title: 2026- MIT Technology Review’s Innovators Under 35
gist: MIT Technology Review's 2026 Innovators Under 35 list selects 35 young scientists and founders from 9 countries and hundreds of nominations, spotlighting deep-tech bets in AI agents, reversible computing, green steel, and age-reversal gene therapy as the areas its editors see as frontier-defining.

insights.claim: MIT Technology Review's newsroom selects 35 young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors each year for its Innovators Under 35 list; the 2026 class was drawn from more than 500 nominations across nine countries with the help of several dozen expert judges.
insights.speaker: MIT Technology Review
insights.so_what: Establishes the list as a curated, judge-vetted signal of where a respected tech publication sees emerging deep-tech talent concentrating, useful as a talent/idea-sourcing screen.
insights.quote: This year's class hails from nine countries and was selected from more than 500 nominations
insights.locator: This year's class hails from nine countries

insights.claim: A separate section of the same package states the 2026 honorees were sifted from 550 nominations, a figure that differs slightly from the '500 nominations' cited in the main intro text of the same piece.
insights.speaker: MIT Technology Review
insights.so_what: A minor internal inconsistency worth flagging when citing the exact nomination count from this source.
insights.quote: Here's what we looked for as we sifted through 550 nominations from around the world.
insights.locator: How we picked 35 of the world's top young scientists

insights.claim: The featured 2026 honorees span biotechnology (Yuancheng (Ryan) Lu's age-reversal gene therapy to restore sight), computing and robotics (Hannah Earley's energy-recycling reversible-computing chips), climate and energy (Laureen Meroueh's cheaper, cleaner steelmaking process), and artificial intelligence (Danijar Hafner's agents that can plan ahead using world models).
insights.speaker: MIT Technology Review
insights.so_what: Signals the specific deep-tech theses (longevity/gene therapy, reversible computing for energy efficiency, green steel, and world-model-based AI agents) the publication views as most investable or field-shifting this year.

insights.claim: The package explicitly frames the honorees' work around confronting 'some of the world's biggest problems, including human disease and climate change,' positioning disease and climate as the two dominant problem categories the editors used to judge significance.
insights.speaker: MIT Technology Review
insights.so_what: Indicates where a mainstream tech-editorial lens expects the largest concentration of high-impact deep-tech founder activity, useful context for thematic portfolio construction.
insights.quote: some of the world's biggest problems, including human disease and climate change
insights.locator: look ahead to the important work that's still before them

themes.theme: Judging Panel as an Institutional Signal

insights.claim: The judging panel includes senior figures spanning AI, robotics, biotech, and materials science, including Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley, Director of the Berkeley Robot Learning Lab), Margaret Mitchell (Hugging Face's chief ethics scientist), James Collins (MIT), Ilan Gur (founding CEO of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency), and William Woodford (cofounder and CTO of Form Energy).
insights.speaker: MIT Technology Review
insights.so_what: The composition of the judging panel itself is a proxy for which institutions and individuals are currently viewed as arbiters of credibility in frontier robotics, AI safety, and energy-storage technology.
